scenes.heading: One Big Table
scenes.narration: The One Big Table approach flattens a star schema into a single wide, denormalized table so that analytical queries can run without joins on fast columnar storage.

scenes.heading: Why teams reach for OBT
bullets: No joins means simpler, faster queries
Columnar formats make wide tables cheap to scan
Easy for analysts and BI tools to consume
Great fit for a single well-known access pattern
scenes.narration: One Big Table eliminates joins by pre-joining facts and dimensions into one flat table, which simplifies queries and speeds them up on columnar engines. Because columnar formats only read the columns a query touches, the extra width costs little at read time. Analysts and BI tools love it because there is nothing to join and the whole entity sits in one place. It shines when there is one dominant, well-understood access pattern the table can be shaped around.

scenes.heading: One Big Table vs star schema
scenes.narration: One Big Table gives join-free, fast, simple reads, but it duplicates dimension attributes across every row and must be rebuilt when a dimension's history or definition changes. A star schema keeps dimensions normalized with little redundancy and flexibly supports many different query shapes, at the cost of joins at query time. Choose One Big Table when a single access pattern dominates and columnar storage makes width cheap; keep a star schema when you need flexibility across diverse, evolving queries.

scenes.heading: Building the wide table
scenes.code:
CREATE TABLE analytics.orders_obt AS
SELECT
  o.order_id, o.order_ts, o.amount,
  c.customer_id, c.customer_name, c.segment, c.region,
  p.product_id, p.product_name, p.category
FROM fact_orders o
JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN dim_product  p ON p.product_id  = o.product_id;
scenes.narration: This statement pre-joins the order fact with the customer and product dimensions to produce a single wide table. Every order row now carries its customer and product attributes inline, so downstream queries need no joins at all. On columnar storage a query touching only a few of these columns reads just those, keeping scans efficient despite the width. The tradeoff is that dimension attributes are duplicated across rows and the table must be refreshed when those attributes change.

scenes.heading: The cost of denormalization
bullets: Schema evolution touches one huge table
scenes.narration: Denormalization is not free. When a dimension attribute changes, that change must be re-propagated to every affected row in the wide table, which can be expensive at scale. Repeating attributes across millions of rows inflates storage, though columnar compression softens the blow. Evolving the schema means altering one enormous table rather than a small dimension. And handling historical versus current attribute values, the kind of thing slowly changing dimensions manage cleanly, becomes muddled unless you design for it explicitly.

scenes.heading: When One Big Table shines
bullets: Columnar engine reads only touched columns
BI users who cannot write joins
scenes.narration: One Big Table is at its best in specific cases. It shines when a single dominant query pattern is known in advance and the table can be shaped around it. It relies on a columnar engine so that its width costs little at read time. It empowers business users and self-service BI tools that struggle with joins, giving them everything in one place. And it maps naturally onto machine-learning feature tables, where a flat, wide row per entity is exactly what training expects.

scenes.text: Flatten to One Big Table when a single access pattern dominates and columnar storage is cheap; keep stars when flexibility wins.
scenes.narration: Reach for One Big Table when a single access pattern dominates and columnar storage makes width cheap, and keep a normalized star schema when you need flexibility across many evolving queries, matching the model to how the data is actually consumed.
